title: Group Size Shapes Nest Emergence Dynamics, Performance and Conservation Implications in Sea Turtle Hatchlings
content:
ABSTRACT

Collective nest emergence in sea turtle hatchlings is an energetically demanding process that can influence post-emergence survival. This study investigates the effect of clutch size on the morphology, physiology, and digging behaviour of green turtle (Chelonia mydas) hatchlings. Sea turtle eggs were collected from Chagar Hutang Turtle Sanctuary in Malaysia between May and September 2023. Eggs were split into large (60 and 40 eggs) and small (15 and 20 eggs) clutches, with experimental incubators mimicking natural nest conditions. Hatchling morphological measurements, glucose levels and self-righting abilities were evaluated, in addition to their digging behaviour recorded using acoustic monitoring during nest emergence. Hatchlings from smaller clutches exhibited larger body and flipper sizes, higher blood glucose levels and shorter self-righting times, indicating higher energy expenditure but enhanced locomotor performance in contrast with hatchlings from larger clutches. Digging duration significantly changed with depth and group size, indicating that larger groups of hatchlings achieve more efficient synchronisation, especially near the sand surface. However, small groups displayed prolonged digging at middle depths, potentially due to reduced coordination and denser sand. These findings suggest that larger clutch sizes facilitate more energy-efficient nest emergence by a collective behaviour, while smaller groups of hatchlings potentially compensate with improved post-emergence performance. These findings indicate that clutch size can influence aspects of collective nest emergence dynamics, but that differences in hatchling morphology and physiology associated with clutch splitting are small and unlikely to have substantial biological consequences, supporting the continued use of clutch-splitting practices in conservation hatcheries. We recommend cautious application of clutch manipulation, balancing emergence efficiency with potential benefits to post-emergence performance.
